cards.text: Paul, the apostle who wrote this letter to the churches of Galatia (Galatians 1:1-2), has been pleading with his friends there. Some of them want to be under the law. So Paul stops and asks them a question, and friend, it's the kind of question your boss asks when he KNOWS you didn't read the email.

cards.question: Paul has a question for the Galatians who want to be under the law. What does he ask them?

answers.text: Do you not understand what the law says
Have you kept every part of the law
Who was the first to teach you the law

cards.text: Then Paul goes right to what's written. Abraham, the man God promised to bless (Genesis 12:1-3), had two sons.

cards.question: Paul says both of Abraham's sons were born to free women.

cards.text: Paul says the two sons were born two very different ways. Back in Genesis, God promised Abraham a son from his wife Sarah in her old age, and Sarah laughed to herself at the idea (Genesis 17:19; 18:11-12).

cards.question: Abraham's son by the slave woman was born according to the ___, but his son by the free woman was born through the ___.

cards.text: Now Paul says these things serve as illustrations: the two women represent two covenants. Buttercup would LOVE this guy, because he's explaining the big stuff with something you can see.

cards.question: Paul says one of the two covenants bears children into slavery. Which mountain does that covenant come from?
Paul says the covenant from Mount Sinai, the one that bears children into slavery, is ___.

cards.text: Hagar was Sarah's Egyptian servant, and she bore Abraham a son (Genesis 16:1, 15). Paul says she stands for Mount Sinai in Arabia and corresponds to the present-day Jerusalem.

cards.question: Why does Paul say Hagar corresponds to the present-day Jerusalem?

answers.text: She is in slavery with her children
She was buried outside its walls
She once lived inside its gates

cards.text: Paul has just tied Hagar to the present-day Jerusalem. Then he says there's ANOTHER Jerusalem, the Jerusalem above, and friend, I can't even keep track of two oven mitts.

cards.question: Paul says the Jerusalem above is in slavery, just like the present-day Jerusalem.

cards.text: Paul says the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother. Then he backs it up with words from the prophet Isaiah (Isaiah 54:1), telling a barren woman who has never had children to rejoice and cry aloud.

cards.question: The words Paul quotes tell the barren woman to rejoice. What reason do they give her?

answers.text: More are the children of the desolate woman
Her husband has finally returned to her
Her fields will soon be fruitful again

cards.text: Now Paul quits talking about Genesis and Isaiah and turns straight to the Galatians. It's like the meeting where the boss finishes the slides, spins around and goes, 'So... about YOU.'

cards.question: Paul tells the Galatian believers that, like ___, they are children of promise.

cards.text: Isaac was the son Sarah bore to Abraham (Genesis 21:2-3). Then Paul goes back one more time to how things went between Abraham's two sons at that time.

cards.question: Paul says that back then, the son born by the flesh did something to the son born by the Spirit. What did he do?
Paul says that trouble between the son born by the flesh and the son born by the Spirit stayed in the past, and it's different now.

cards.text: So what's to be done? Paul asks, 'But what does the Scripture say?' and quotes it: 'Expel the slave woman and her son.'

cards.question: The Scripture Paul quotes says to expel the slave woman and her son. What reason does it give?

answers.text: Her son will never share in the inheritance
Her son broke the rules of the household
Her son was old enough to live on his own

cards.question: Paul ends by telling the believers that they are children of the slave woman.

findings.problem: Most story cards are plain narration with no Papa Dorin voice: stop 1 cards 3, 5 and 10, and stop 2 cards 3, 7 and 10. There are only about four jokes across 23 cards, so the walkthrough mostly reads like a pleasant narrator, not a laugh-out-loud storyteller.

rule.text: When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.

findings.problem: "has been pleading with his friends there" is a Bible fact from the earlier part of the letter (Galatians 4:12-20), but it has no reference. Only the line about who wrote the letter cites Galatians 1:1-2.

rule.text: Every Bible fact he states carries its reference.

findings.problem: Blank 1 ("flesh") tests exact wording the baker hasn't seen. Nothing on the earlier cards lets a baker reason toward "flesh" for the slave woman's son. Card 5 only sets up the promise side.

rule.text: The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: The wrong answer "law" is arguable for blank 1. Paul ties the slave woman to the covenant from Mount Sinai (Galatians 4:24-25), and card 1 frames the passage around being under the law. A baker could argue the slave woman's son was born "according to the law."

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: The right answer "More are the children of the desolate woman" keeps the Bible's old-fashioned word order. The wrong answers ("Her husband has finally returned to her", "Her fields will soon be fruitful again") use plain modern wording, so the right answer stands out.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: Isaac is never named on any earlier card, so a baker can't reason their way to him over Ishmael or Esau without outside knowledge. He is only introduced on card 7, after the question. Card 5 of stop 1 could name Sarah's promised son Isaac (Genesis 17:19), which would make this an informed guess.

rule.text: The check: could a thoughtful baker who has only seen the earlier cards make a reasoned pick? If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question.
